comment: The boards wz's Zephyr images are built for, one row per BOARD x LINK x APP, and how far each row is WITNESSED. This file is the one place that says so; deploy/zephyr-*/boards/*.conf are the per-board settings it names, and scripts/lib/zephyr_board_table_gate.py reads both.

A claim goes no higher than the LOWEST grade its evidence reaches. DECLARED: the board is a target, nothing was built. BUILT: hosted CI builds the image for this row (Layer Qzb) and nothing has run it. QEMU: the image boots on an emulated machine and a lane reads a verdict from it (witness.lane). HARDWARE: someone ran it on the board and a ledger entry records what ran (image hash, verdict sentence, date, who).

HARDWARE needs a lab. wz publishes the image and the verdict-sentence grammar; whoever owns the board runs it and files the record. Until that record exists in the store the row stays at BUILT, however likely it looks.
A board's RMII and its 10BASE-T1S port are different rows: they are different links with different drivers, and one can be witnessed while the other is not.

A board that runs more than one image lists the others under companions, and a row names what it needs in requires: a row's claim goes no higher than the lowest grade of what it runs with. A HARDWARE row and its HARDWARE companions cite the one ledger entry, because what ran was the images together, and the entry names each image's hash and every step of the app's HARDWARE_VERDICT.md that the row names (a row names all of them unless its verdict_steps narrows it to the steps its record was made against).

witness.verdict: HW.0 to HW.7 held on the pair of images, each step ending OK
witness.by: the lab session of the bench host the board is attached to, with the owner's permission

rows.note: The image is for the M7_0 core, and on this chip only the CM0+ core starts by itself: Zephyr's board documentation says CM7_0 runs only when a CM0+ application enables it (Cy_SysEnableCM7). The clock tree is the CM0+ image's job too: Zephyr's clock driver on the M7 returns without configuring it (drivers/clock_control/clock_control_infineon.c). The CM0+ image wz builds for this is the companion listed below. On a bench kit whose existing CM0+ image started CM7_0 without configuring the clocks, the M7 ran at about 8 MHz where the build assumes 350 MHz, so the kernel's clock ran about 44 times slow (measured: 229 ticks per second against the configured 10000, a cycle counter at 8.02 MHz), and the first boot printed nothing past the probe for 100 seconds of wall time, which was about 2 seconds of kernel time. The image now reads the core clock from the clock registers before it waits for anything, logs it (wz: core clock N Hz) and stops with a FAIL line when it is more than 2 percent off the build's, so that state is refused instead of silent; the MAC driver's waits are also bounded by the kernel clock now, not counted. HARDWARE is the record's run of the two images together on a bench kit, the whole verdict of deploy/zephyr-admin-node/HARDWARE_VERDICT.md as it was then (HW.0 to HW.7, the row's verdict_steps; the later steps are the second interface's and this image does not carry it): the core clock read 350000000 Hz, the link came up at 100 Mbps full duplex, the node answered 6 of 6 pings, two stock routers saw it as a peer, it dialled the second when told to and refused a group of two. Its main stack peaked at 20284 of 32768 bytes, which passes the rule of a quarter free and uses 62 percent of it. What the record does not settle: a start after the board's power is removed completely, and a DMA bus width other than the chip's 64 bits.

The image with the SPI probe: SCB3 opened as a master on the MikroBUS socket (through the PDL; the pinned Zephyr's own SPI binding is unusable on this chip) and the identity registers read and logged at boot: the two standard TC6 ones (OA_ID, OA_PHYID) and the LAN8650/1's own DEVID, which the standard ones cannot replace. A lab ran the first two on a bench kit with a 10BASE-T1S click plugged in and reported OA_ID 0x00000011 and OA_PHYID 0x0007c1b4, at two boots. The lab gave the first 16 hex digits of the image's sha256, no verdict grammar exists for this row yet, and the DEVID read did not exist, so the row stays BUILT. What that image did after those lines is on the RMII row. Nothing is plugged into the socket on a kit as shipped.

The image with both interfaces on one lwIP stack: the onboard RMII port and a Microchip LAN8650/1 on a 10BASE-T1S expansion board in the MikroBUS socket, which is an expansion board rather than a device of the kit (its Lite user guide names no 10BASE-T1S part, and the socket is not populated by default). The second interface is the SCB3 SPI master (wz-spi-scb over the PDL), the chip's bring-up (wz-eth-lan865x over wz-oa-tc6, which identifies the part by DEVID and refuses a model or silicon revision no document grades rather than apply another revision's configuration) and a second port of the node, added after the onboard one so that the node's id and the default route stay the onboard port's; the node listens on both and advertises a locator for each. Layer Qzb builds it with overlays/t2g_t1s_build_values.conf, which holds numbers made up so that the build is whole (a PLCA id and count, an address, both control lines stated wired) and describes no board: the Kconfig gives none of them a default, so a build that forgets one fails by name, and a lab states its own. The kit's side is read from its board support package and the PDL (the socket's SPI pins, SCB3, and the pins the socket puts RST and INT on); what the expansion board connects to the socket is the lab's to state and is not read from anything here. Nothing has run on silicon: not the chip's reply to the bring-up with PLCA, not a frame on the wire, not the SPI clock above the probe's. The row stays BUILT until a lab's record exists, and HARDWARE_VERDICT.md would need steps for the second interface first: its steps put the node's answers to one locator.

witness.verdict: CM7_0 started by it, wz_launcher_status 1, the M7_0 image at its built clock
witness.by: the lab session of the bench host the board is attached to, with the owner's permission

companions.note: The image the kit's CM0+ core runs so that the M7_0 image runs at the speed it was built for: Zephyr's own clock driver brings the clock tree up from the board's devicetree in a CM0+ build, and the launcher then starts CM7_0 at the start of the M7_0 flash partition, which the launcher reads from the same devicetree node the M7_0 image is linked at. It replaces whatever CM0+ image the kit carried. It prints nothing: the kit's console (SCB0) belongs to the M7_0 image, and on the first run, with both cores on it, the launcher's banner came out cut and garbled and none of its lines reached the console. Its own verdict is a word in its RAM, wz_launcher_status, that a debugger reads (0 running, 1 CM7_0 started, 2 no M7_0 image found, 3 CM7_0 power mode not taken within the limit); the evidence a console can carry is the M7_0 image's, which logs the core clock it measured at boot. The record the companion cites is the one its row cites, because what ran was the two images together: after a reset with the debugger session closed, wz_launcher_status read 1, the M7_0 image measured 349.5 MHz and 9987 kernel ticks per second against 10000 configured, and the node ran the whole verdict.
